# Cleaning an espresso machine

An espresso machine needs regular cleaning to keep its shots tasting clean. Coffee oils build up on the group head and in the portafilter basket every day. After a week those oils turn rancid, and the stale flavour shows up in every cup you pull, even with fresh beans.

The daily routine takes about five minutes. After the last shot, lock an empty portafilter with a blind basket into the group head and run water through it for ten seconds. Wipe the shower screen with a damp cloth while the machine is still warm, because dried coffee is much harder to remove later in the evening.

Once a week the machine needs a deeper clean with a detergent made for espresso equipment. Put a small spoonful of the powder into the blind basket and run the pump in short bursts so the solution reaches the valve behind the group head. Rinse the basket well afterwards and pull one shot to throw away before you drink anything.

Hard water causes a slower problem. Minerals settle inside the boiler and the pipes over months, and a thick layer of scale makes the heating element work harder while the water flow drops. How often you need to descale depends on the hardness of the local water supply, so check the label on your machine or ask the supplier.

The steam wand needs care after every use as well. Milk dries inside the tip within minutes and blocks the small holes that make the foam. Purge the wand for two seconds before and after steaming, then wipe it with a clean cloth that you keep only for this job.

A clean machine also lasts longer. Many repairs on home machines start with scale or old coffee that blocked a valve, and those repairs often cost more than a year of cleaning supplies would have cost in the first place.
